issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
For Amir, the moment that shattered everything happened on a Tuesday evening. He had been the first paramedic on scene after a multi-car collision on the interstate, and he had recognized the car. It was his brother-in-law’s sedan, crumpled against the guardrail. Amir had pulled him from the wreckage, working with a calm he no longer recognizes in himself, applying pressure to the wounds that would not stop bleeding. He remembers the antiseptic smell of the hospital bay where he finally handed him off to the trauma team, the sharp chemical scent that now seems to follow him everywhere. He remembers the terror in his own chest, a feeling that did not leave when the doctors told him his brother-in-law would survive. What Amir cannot remember, no matter how hard he tries, are the minutes between recognizing the car and getting him onto the stretcher. There are gaps in his memory that feel like missing pieces of himself, and when the memory does come back—which it does, without warning—it returns in full, vivid color, every smell and sound and sensation arriving at once, as if he is still there on the asphalt with blood on his gloves. The terror that grips him in those moments is the same terror he felt then, undiminished by time.

In the weeks and months that followed, Amir became convinced that he had permanently changed for the worse. He could feel it in his bones. Before the accident, he had trusted his instincts, his hands, his ability to stay calm under pressure. Now he cannot rely on himself. He replays the scene obsessively, searching for something he could have done differently, and the conclusion is always the same: he should have protected his brother-in-law, and he failed. This belief has settled into him like a weight. He tries hard not to think about it, pushing the memories away when they surface, but suppression only seems to make them return more forcefully. So he has adopted another strategy: he throws himself into work. He volunteers for extra shifts, takes the most difficult calls, fills every quiet moment with tasks. Overworking keeps his mind occupied, but it also means he is constantly exposed to the very things that trigger him. Visible injuries on strangers—a gash on a child’s arm, a wound being bandaged—send him reeling. He sees the faces of victims he has treated, unbidden, at the worst possible moments. And the smell of the hospital, the antiseptic that hangs in every corridor, has become a permanent part of his sensory landscape, a reminder he cannot escape.

At home, his wife has noticed the changes. He reacts with alarm when she touches him unexpectedly, sometimes flinching or pulling away before he can stop himself. He has started choosing where to sit in every room based on how safe or protected he feels—his back to a wall, a clear view of the door, a position from which no one can approach him unseen. He has difficulty concentrating, finding that his mind drifts mid-conversation, that he loses the thread of television shows, that he cannot focus on the dinner table talk that used to ground him. He has stopped wanting to go to work, though he goes anyway, because the thought of staying home with nothing to occupy his hands feels worse. The avoidance is not a choice he makes consciously; it is a reflex. He dreads the start of every shift, and yet he cannot imagine stopping, because stopping would mean sitting still with what he carries.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was not the flashbacks or the fear or the sleepless nights. It was a moment at his daughter’s birthday party, when he saw a small scrape on her knee and felt his chest seize, his vision narrow, his mouth go dry. He excused himself and sat in the bathroom for ten minutes, trying to breathe. He realized then that he could no longer trust himself to be present for the people he loved. He is afraid that the damage is permanent, that he will never feel like himself again. But he is also hoping, in a quiet way he does not yet know how to put into words, that someone can help him find a way back.
